question: According to studies cited in the manual, what do most crash-involved riders do wrong with the brakes?
choice_a: Underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear
choice_b: Overbrake the front tire and underbrake the rear
choice_c: Use both brakes equally and correctly
choice_d: Refuse to use the rear brake at all
explanation: Studies show that most crash-involved riders underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear, and often did not separate braking from swerving or did not choose swerving when appropriate.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.29, 'Crash Avoidance'

question: What is the correct technique for a quick stop?
choice_a: Use only the rear brake to avoid locking the front wheel
choice_b: Apply both brakes at the same time, squeezing the front brake lever firmly and progressively without grabbing it
choice_c: Grab the front brake lever as hard as possible instantly
choice_d: Coast to a stop without using either brake
explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time; squeeze the brake lever firmly and progressively, and don't be shy about using the front brake, but don't "grab" it either.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.29, 'Quick Stops'

question: What should a rider do if the front wheel locks during a quick stop?
choice_a: Keep the front brake locked until stopped
choice_b: Switch entirely to the rear brake for the remainder of the stop
choice_c: Release the front brake lever immediately, then reapply it firmly
explanation: If the front wheel locks, release the front brake lever immediately then reapply it firmly, while at the same time pressing down on the rear brake.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.29, 'Quick Stops'

question: If the rear wheel accidentally locks on a good-traction surface during a stop, what can a rider do?
choice_a: Immediately let go of the rear brake and swerve
choice_c: It will always cause an immediate crash with no exceptions
choice_d: Keep it locked until completely stopped, since even with a locked rear wheel you can control the motorcycle if it is upright and going straight
explanation: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped; even with a locked rear wheel, you can control the motorcycle if it is upright and going in a straight line.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.29, 'Quick Stops'

question: If you must stop quickly while in a curve, what should you do first if the situation allows?
choice_a: First straighten and square the handlebars, then stop
choice_b: Brake as hard as possible while still fully leaned over
choice_c: Never brake at all while in a curve, under any circumstance
choice_d: Accelerate through the curve before braking
explanation: If you must stop quickly while in a curve, first straighten and square the handlebars, then stop, if the situation allows.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.29, 'Stopping Quickly in a Curve'

question: If you can't straighten the handlebars first when stopping quickly in a curve (such as facing a danger of running off the road), what should you do?
choice_a: Apply maximum brake pressure immediately regardless of lean angle
choice_b: Apply the brakes smoothly and gradually, reducing lean angle as you slow and applying more brake pressure as more traction becomes available
choice_c: Release the throttle only and coast without braking
choice_d: Swerve sharply first, then brake while still swerving
explanation: If conditions don't allow straightening first, apply the brakes smoothly and gradually rather than with as much force as if upright; as you slow, reduce lean angle and apply more brake pressure until the motorcycle is straight and maximum brake pressure can be applied.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.29, 'Stopping Quickly in a Curve'

question: What is a "swerve," and when should braking be combined with it?
choice_a: A swerve always requires braking at the same instant for maximum control
choice_b: A swerve is the same maneuver as maximum straight-line braking
choice_c: A swerve is a sudden change in direction; if the situation allows, separate braking from swerving -- brake before or after, never while making an aggressive swerve
choice_d: Swerving should never be combined with any braking, ever
explanation: A swerve is a sudden change in direction, used when there isn't enough room to stop. If the situation allows, separate braking from swerving -- brake before or after, never while making an aggressive swerve.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.29-30, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: How should a rider apply handgrip pressure to swerve?
choice_a: Pull back evenly on both handgrips
choice_b: Turn the handlebars sharply as if steering a car
choice_d: Apply a small amount of hand pressure to the handgrip on the side of the intended direction of escape, causing the motorcycle to lean quickly
explanation: To swerve, apply a small amount of hand pressure to the handgrip located on the side of your intended direction of escape; this will cause the motorcycle to lean quickly, and the sharper the desired turn, the more the motorcycle must lean.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.30, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: During maximum straight-line braking, where should a rider keep their body and eyes?
choice_a: Body centered over the motorcycle, looking well ahead, not down
choice_b: Leaning far forward with eyes fixed on the front wheel
choice_c: Body positioned as far back as possible with eyes closed
choice_d: It doesn't matter where you look while braking hard
explanation: Keep your body centered over the motorcycle and look well ahead, not down -- this helps keep the motorcycle as straight as possible, minimizing lean angle and the likelihood of the tires losing traction.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.30, 'Maximum Straight-Line Braking'

question: What happens if the front wheel locks and the rider fails to fully release the front brake lever immediately?
choice_b: It will result in a crash, since front-wheel skids cause immediate loss of steering control and balance
choice_c: The rear wheel will automatically compensate
choice_d: The motorcycle will simply slow down more quickly with no downside
explanation: Front-wheel skids result in immediate loss of steering control and balance; failure to fully release the brake lever immediately will result in a crash.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.30, 'Front-Wheel Skids'

question: What is a "high-side" crash?
choice_a: A crash that only happens on highways with high speed limits
choice_b: A minor low-speed tip-over with no rider injury
choice_c: It occurs when the wheels are out of alignment and a locked rear wheel is released, causing the motorcycle to snap upright and throw the rider into the air
choice_d: A crash caused exclusively by front-wheel skids
explanation: A high-side crash occurs when the wheels are out of alignment and a locked rear wheel is released -- the motorcycle can abruptly snap upright, throwing the rider into the air ahead of the motorcycle's path.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.30-31, 'Rear-Wheel Skids'

question: What is a primary cause of single-vehicle crashes in curves, according to the manual?
choice_a: Motorcycles being too narrow for the lane
choice_b: Excessive use of the front brake before entering a curve
choice_d: Motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn
explanation: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn; every curve is different, so ride within your skill level and posted speed limits.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.31, 'Curves'

question: Where does the manual suggest a rider position within the lane before entering a curve, and why?
choice_a: Move to the center of the lane before entering the curve and stay there until exiting, to spot approaching traffic as soon as possible
choice_b: Always hug the outside edge of the lane regardless of traffic
choice_c: Position doesn't matter as long as speed is controlled
choice_d: Ride in the oncoming lane for a better view
explanation: A good choice is to move to the center of your lane before entering a curve and stay there until you exit -- this permits you to spot approaching traffic as soon as possible and adjust for traffic crowding the center line.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.31-32, 'Curves'
